'''''Salix purpurea''''', known in Britain as '''purple willow''', is a shrub or small tree native to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa. It has been introduced to many other parts of the world as an ornamental garden plant, and it is widely used in basket making. Within its native range and some places where it is naturalised it is found in wetlands such as lake margins and the floodplains of rivers.

==Description==
Purple willow is a dioecious shrub or small tree up to about 5 m tall, usually with numerous stems. The bark is greyish and smooth, with a bitter taste. The vegetative parts of the plant are all [[Glabrousness|glabrous]]. The twigs and young branches are [[terete]] and flexible, often yellowish or tinged with purple.

The leaves are - unusually, for a willow - opposite or almost opposite and narrowly oblong in shape, with a pointed tip, ranging from 2 cm to about 10 cm long. In bud, each leaf is covered by a single scale. They are a characteristically dull, pale green when fresh, turning black if the stems are harvested. The margins are entire or slightly serrated towards the tip. The [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] are very short and the stipules usually fall early.
[[File:Salix purpurea shoot.jpg|thumb|The leaves can be alternate, subopposite or (very rarely) almost in whorls of three]]

Catkins appear before the leaves in the spring, and have either male or female flowers (on separate plants). They are narrowly cylindrical and usually held upright, about 3 cm long by 0.5 cm wide. Each catkin is typically subtended by 2 or 3 small bracts. The [[rhachis]] is densely hairy, as are the black catkin scales, which are bracteoles subtending each flower. The perianth (sepals and petals) is reduced to 1-2 tiny nectaries. The male catkins have flowers with 2 long stamens, exceeding the scales, and red anthers which open at maturity to reveal bright yellow pollen; the female ones have 2 bifid stigmas on a very short style. The fruit is a capsule about 4 mm long by half as wide, with a plume of hairs arising from the base.<ref name=Meikle1984>{{Cite book |last=Meikle |first=R.D. |title=Willows and Poplars of Great Britain and Ireland |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |year=1984 |isbn=0-901158-07-0}}</ref><ref name=Stace2019>{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=C & M Floristics |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |edition=4th |location=Middlewood Green}}</ref>
<ref name=Sell2018>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 1 |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0-521-55335-3}}</ref>
[[File:Salix purpurea (Purpur-Weide) IMG 34491.JPG|thumb|The male catkins have red anthers]]
[[File:Salix purpurea (Purpur-Weide) IMG 35532.JPG|thumb|Female catkins]]

==Taxonomy==
The scientific name ''Salix purpurea'' was given by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in 1753, in [[Species Plantarum]], vol. 2, p. 1017. He gave as a synonym his own polynomial description from ''Iter Scanicum'', his report on a journey through the Swedish countryside in 1749. He wrote "''Salix foliis serratis glabris-lanceolatis: inferioribus oppositis''" (the willow with serrated, glabrous, lanceolate leaves, the lower ones being opposite). He also quoted [[John Ray]], who described it as "''Salix folio longo subluteo non auriculata, viminibus rubris''" (the willow with long yellowish leaves, no auricles, and red stems).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linné |first=Carl von |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13830 |title=Caroli Linnaei ... Species plantarum :exhibentes plantas rite cognitas, ad genera relatas, cum differentiis specificis, nominibus trivialibus, synonymis selectis, locis natalibus, secundum systema sexuale digestas... |last2=Linné |first2=Carl von |last3=Salvius |first3=Lars |date=1753 |publisher=Impensis Laurentii Salvii |volume= 2 |location=Holmiae}}</ref>

The name ''Salix'' is an ancient [[Proto-Indo-European language|Proto-Indo-European]] word for willow which comes down to modern English as "sallow." It was a word in Roman times, probably [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/salix#Latin derived from Gallic]: [[Pliny the Elder]] used it in his ''[[Natural History (Pliny)|Naturalis Historia]]'', but it may not have been in common use, because [[Dioscorides]] did not; his word for willow was "iter".<ref name=Dioscorides>{{cite web |vauthors = Dioscorides P |author-link=Pedanius Dioscorides |title=De Materia Medica |url=https://archive.org/details/dioscorides-de-materia-medica-2000-english}}</ref> The epithet ''purpurea'' simply means purple-coloured, which could refer to the male flowers or to the stems and leaves, which can have a distinctly purplish tinge, especially as they dry.

Other common names for purple willow include purpleosier willow,<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SAPU2|taxon=Salix purpurea|accessdate=27 October 2015}}</ref> and purple osier.

Its [[ploidy|chromosome number]] is ''2n'' = 38.<ref name="Stace2019"/>

Purple willow is part of a complex of related species and there have been many attempts to create a coherent taxonomy. It is a combination of two Linnaean species, as the modern concept includes ''Salix helix'' <small>L.</small>. Leaves vary from narrowly oblong to more broadly ovate; some varieties have serrated leaves while others are entire; and the colour of the stems is highly variable. The female flowers have also been used to describe separate taxa: some have bifid stigmas while others are ovate.<ref name="Meikle1984" /> The current understanding is that the numerous forms that occur in central and eastern Asia are different species, whereas ''S. purpurea'' accounts only for the European and North African plants, and just reaches into western Asia, but not as far as Moscow.<ref name=Skvortsov2023>{{Cite journal |last=Skvortsov |first=A.K. |title=Materials on Morphology and Systematics of Salicaceae. XII. Salix purpurea L. and Related Species |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/381135789_Materials_on_Morphology_and_Systematics_of_Salicaceae_XII_Salix_purpurea_L_and_Related_Species |journal=Skvortsovia |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=29-48 | year=2023 |doi=10.51776/2309-6500_2023_9_1_29 |via=Researchgate}}</ref> Just four subspecies and forms are currently accepted:<ref name = powo>{{cite web |title=''Salix purpurea'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:301321-2 |website=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=12 February 2025}}</ref>
*''Salix purpurea'' subsp. ''eburnea'' {{small|(Borzì) Cif. & Giacom. ex S.Pignatti}} – Sardinia
*''S. purpurea'' f. ''gracilis'' {{small|Wimm.}} – Belgium, Germany, Poland, Switzerland, and Spain
*''S. purpurea'' subsp. ''leucodermis'' {{small|Yalt.}} – Turkey
*''S. purpurea'' subsp. ''purpurea'' – Europe, the Caucasus, Turkey, and northwestern Africa
[[File:Salix purpurea female flowers.jpg|thumb|Close-up of the female flowers, showing the bifid stigmas characteristic of some varieties]]

==Distribution and status==
The native range is southern Europe and north Africa, extending as far north as Denmark and eastwards to [[Turkey]] and the [[Baltic states]]. It is only just in western Russia: plants further east are a different species in the ''Salix purpurea'' group. Britain may be at the northern edge of its range, or it might be introduced there, as it is thought to be in Scandinavia.<ref name ="powo" /> It has also been introduced into many other parts of the world, mostly as an ornamental plant.<ref name=gbif>{{Cite web |title=Salix purpurea L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5372800 |access-date=2025-12-19 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref> It is naturalised in wetlands in North America.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Salix purpurea in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242417203 |access-date=2025-12-19 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref>

Its altitudinal range is from sea level to 1,400 m in Britain, to 2,000 m in the Alps and the [[Pyrenees]], and as high as 2,500 m at the southern edge of its range, in the [[Atlas mountains]].<ref name="Skvortsov2023" />

Its status globally and in Britain is LC ([[Least-concern species|least concern]]).<ref name=iucn>{{Cite iucn |title=''Salix purpurea'' |author=Rivers, M.C., Mark, J. & Khela, S. |name-list-style=amp |article-number= e.T203471A68107793 |date=2017 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2017-3.RLTS.T203471A68107793.en |access-date=11 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.m2v |access-date=2025-12-20 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref> In most counties in Britain it is considered an [[axiophyte]] because it is restricted to wetlands with a high conservation value, whether it is native there or not.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/learn/getting-started/terms/general-terms/axiophytes |access-date=2025-12-20 |website=bsbi.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
Within its native range of southern Europe and north Africa, purple willow is most characteristic of the EUNIS habitat F9.122 ''Western Mediterranean purple willow scrub'', which comprises stands of purple, [[Salix eleagnos|olive]]- and [[Salix triandra|almond willow]] lining watercourses.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EUNIS -Factsheet for Western Mediterranean purple willow scrub |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/habitats/4830 |access-date=2025-12-22 |website=eunis.eea.europa.eu}}</ref>

It is also found in riverside scrub in Britain and northern France.<ref name=Chater2010>{{cite book |last=Chater |first=A.O. |title=Flora of Cardiganshire |date=2010 |publisher=A.O. Chater |location=Aberystwyth |isbn=9-780956-575005}}</ref><ref name=Maskew2014>{{Cite book |last=Maskew |first=Roger |title=The Flora of Worcestershire |publisher=Roger Maskew |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-9926693-0-0 |location=Stoke Bliss}}</ref><ref name=Guillemot2023>{{Cite book |last=Guillemot |first=Vincent |title=Flore du Massif armoricain et ses marges |publisher=Editions Biotope |year=2023 |isbn=978-2-36662-301-7 |location=Mèze |language=fr}}</ref> In Britain this is classified as [[British NVC community W6|W6 ''Salix fragilis'']] woodland. Here it could possibly be native or is more likely to have been planted, as [[osier bed]]s were often cultivated within floodplains.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |title=The Flora of Stodmarsh National Nature Reserve |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-of-stodmarsh-2022 |website=Internet Archive |access-date=23 January 2022}}</ref> Another native habitat for it is beside lakes such as the ancient glacial lakes of the [[Meres and Mosses]] region of the Shropshire-Cheshire plain. Here it grows in [[British NVC community W1|grey willow carr]], sometimes in standing water, and is considered an indicator of ancient woodland.<ref name=Lockton2015>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref><ref name=Rodwell1>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 1: woodlands and scrub |year=1991 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref> In France its habitat is very similar.<ref name=Guillemot2023>{{Cite book |last=Guillemot |first=Vincent |title=Flore du Massif armoricain et ses marges |publisher=Editions Biotope |year=2023 |isbn=978-2-36662-301-7 |location=Mèze |language=fr}}</ref>
[[File:Salix purpurea Bomere Pool.jpg|thumb|Purple willow on the margin of Bomere Pool, Shropshire]]

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg-type indicator values]] are L=8, F=8, R=8, N=5 and S=0, which show that it has a preference for bright sunlight, very wet conditions, base-rich water, low fertility and no salinity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tichý |first=Lubomír |last2=Axmanová |first2=Irena |last3=Dengler |first3=Jürgen |last4=Guarino |first4=Riccardo |last5=Jansen |first5=Florian |last6=Midolo |first6=Gabriele |last7=Nobis |first7=Michael P. |last8=Van Meerbeek |first8=Koenraad |last9=Aćić |first9=Svetlana |last10=Attorre |first10=Fabio |last11=Bergmeier |first11=Erwin |last12=Biurrun |first12=Idoia |last13=Bonari |first13=Gianmaria |last14=Bruelheide |first14=Helge |last15=Campos |first15=Juan Antonio |year=2023 |title=Ellenberg-type indicator values for European vascular plant species |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jvs.13168 |journal=Journal of Vegetation Science |volume=34 |issue=1 |article-number=e13168 |doi=10.1111/jvs.13168 |issn=1100-9233|hdl=11475/26829 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

There are many organisms associated with purple willow. The Plant Parasites of Europe website<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superrosids/rosids/fabids/malpighiales/salicaceae/salix/salix-purpurea/ |access-date=2025-12-20 | title=Plant Parasites of Europe |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref> lists 247 species, of which 209 are insects, 25 [[Fungus|fungi]], 12 [[mite]]s and one a [[Chromista|single-celled organism]]. Among the insects are 39 species of [[beetle]], 62 [[Hemiptera|true bugs]], 23 [[Hymenoptera|bees, wasps and ants]] and 61 [[Lepidoptera]] (butterflies or moths).<ref name=redfern2002>{{cite journal |last1=Redfern |first1=Margaret |last2=Shirley |first2=Peter |title=British Plant Galls |journal=Field Studies |date=2002 |volume=10 |pages=207-531 |isbn=1 85153 214 5}}</ref>

Three of these may be monophagous on purple willow:
*''[[Euura salicispurpureae]]'' is a mite which produces galls in young shoots of purple willow and its hybrids
*''[[Aculus truncatus]]'' is another species of mite which galls the leaf margins of purple willow, causing curling
*''[[Rabdophaga purpureaperda]]'' is a midge which forms galls in the tips of shoots

Other significant parasites include:
*The sawfly ''[[Euura proxima]]'', which produces red bean-shaped swellings on the upper surface of the leaves of this and other willows
*''[[Euura viminalis]]'', which creates spherical pale green galls on the lower surface of the leaves of purple willow or [[Salix viminalis|common osier]]
*''[[Rabdophaga degeerii]]'', which causes swellings in the shoots in northern Britain
*The [[poplar hawkmoth]], whose larvae feed on willow leaves.
[[File:POPLAR HAWKMOTH Laothoe populi (6271114661).jpg|thumb|Poplar hawkmoth caterpillar (shown here on a poplar shoot)]]

Willows are largely insect-pollinated, and the flowers produce a distinctive scent to attract various bees, flies and other pollinators. They are considered a useful source of nectar for sustaining insect populations early in the year.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ostaff |first=D. P. |last2=Mosseler |first2=A. |last3=Johns |first3=R. C. |last4=Javorek |first4=S. |last5=Klymko |first5=J. |last6=Ascher |first6=J. S. |year=2015 |title=Willows (Salix spp.) as pollen and nectar sources for sustaining fruit and berry pollinating insects |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/full/10.4141/cjps-2014-339 |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=95 |issue=3 |pages=505–516 |doi=10.4141/cjps-2014-339 |issn=0008-4220|url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, there is some evidence that willows can be wind-pollinated as well.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Argus |first=George W. |year=1974 |title=An experimental study of hybridization and pollination in Salix (willow) |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/abs/10.1139/b74-212 |journal=Canadian Journal of Botany |volume=52 |issue=7 |pages=1613–1619 |doi=10.1139/b74-212 |issn=0008-4026}}</ref>

==Uses==
Purple willow has long been used for basket making and is still harvested for that purpose, when it is often known as "Brittany Green" willow, valued for its purple colour and evenly-sized stems (i.e. remaining the same thickness along its length).<ref>{{Cite web |title=What type of willow is used in basket weaving? |url=https://www.musgrovewillows.co.uk/help-and-advice/what-type-of-willow-is-used-in-basket-weaving/ |access-date=2025-12-20 |website=Musgrove Willows |language=en-gb}}</ref> Willow beds were often planted with a variety of plants: the British botanist Charles Sinker documented a withy bed at Crew Green in Wales which contained five species and three hybrids.<ref name=Sinker1985>{{Cite book |last1=Sinker |first1=C.A. |title=Ecological Flora of the Shropshire Region |last2=Packham |first2=J.R. |last3=Trueman |first3=I.C |last4=Oswald |first4=P.H. |last5=Perring |first5=F.H. |last6=Prestwood |first6=W.V. |publisher=Shropshire Wildlife Trust |year=1985 |isbn=0 95086 371 8 |location=Shrewsbury}}</ref>

The weeping cultivar 'Pendula' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/97778/i-Salix-purpurea-i-Pendula/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Salix purpurea'' 'Pendula' | access-date = 12 October 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 93 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 12 October 2018}}</ref> As with several other willows, the shoots, called [[withy|withies]], are often used in [[basket]]ry. The wood of this and other willow species is used in making [[cricket bat]]s.

The Roman herbalist [[Dioscorides]] had many uses for ''iter'' (willow): taken with pepper and wine it would help people with intestinal obstruction, or effect birth control, and the juice of the leaves (with other ingredients) would help sores in the ears. The bark, when burned and mixed with vinegar, would take away calluses and corns.<ref name= "Dioscorides" /> [[Nicholas Culpeper|Culpeper]] suggested that the boughs of willow, stuck about a chamber, would refresh those who had fevers.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Culpeper |first1=Nicholas |title=The Complete Herbal |date=1850 |publisher=Thomas Kelly |location=London |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513}}</ref>

More recent herbalists have had less use for willow. [[Maud Grieve|Mrs Grieve]] did not mention purple willow at all.<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |year=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref> This could be because the effects of consumption can include gastrointestinal bleeding and kidney damage,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Salix purpurea Purple Osier. purpleosier willow PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Salix+purpurea |access-date=2025-12-18 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref> and just eating the leaves can cause severe abdominal pain.<ref name=poison>{{cite book |last1=Cooper |first1=M.R. |last2=Johnson |first2=A.W. |last3=Dauncey |first3=E.A. |title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi |date=2003 |publisher=The Stationery Office |location=London |isbn=0-11-702861-4}}</ref>
